chapterNote: The psalm of the God who is never not there, and never not looking — theology's grandest doctrines sung in the first person. Four stanzas of six verses. First, omniscience made personal: You have searched me and known me — sitting, rising, thoughts from afar, the word on my tongue before I say it, hemmed in behind and before, and the psalmist's honest verdict: such knowledge is too wonderful for me. Second, omnipresence tested by every escape route: heaven, Sheol, the wings of the dawn to the sea's far side, the dark itself — and every road ends at the same place, 'You are there,' until darkness and light are both alike to Him. Third, the reason He knows me so completely: He made me — kidneys and frame acquired and knit in the womb's hidden place, embroidered like fine needlework, every day of the life written in His book before one of them existed. It is Scripture's great charter of the unborn, and of every life that has ever been dismissed as unfinished. Fourth, the hard stanza softened by its ending: David's zeal against God's enemies pivots into the prayer that gives the whole psalm its use — Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my anxious thoughts; see if there is any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. The God who searches cannot be escaped; the psalmist's genius is to stop running and invite the search.

1.text: For the choir director. A psalm of David. O LORD, You have searched me through, and You know me.
1.amp: To the chief Musician [natsach], A Psalm [mizmor] of David. O LORD [YHWH], You have searched [chaqar — explored, examined to the bottom] me, and known [yada] me.
1.notes: chaqar (H2713) is the deep-search verb — prospecting a mine, sounding a depth (cf. Job 28:3). The exploration is finished ('have searched') and the file complete: yada (H3045), known — the psalm opens where most theology ends.

2.text: You know when I sit down and when I rise up; You discern my thought from far away.
2.amp: You know [yada] my downsitting [yashab] and my uprising [qum], You understand [bin] my thought [rea] afar off [rachoq].
2.notes: The day's two hinges, yashab and qum (H3427, H6965) — and everything between them. bin (H995) is discernment: the thought read at rachoq (H7350), from far off, while it is still forming, before its owner has finished thinking it.

3.text: You sift my path and my lying down, and You are thoroughly acquainted with all my ways.
3.amp: You compass ['winnowest', zarah, the KJV margin — sift as grain] my path [orach] and my lying down [reba], and are acquainted [sakan — intimately familiar] with all my ways [derek].
3.notes: zarah (H2219) is winnowing: the path tossed and sifted until every grain of it is sorted. Waking travel (orach, H734) and sleep both audited, and sakan (H5532) is the familiarity of long acquaintance — God knows my ways the way a craftsman knows his own tools.

4.text: For there is not a word on my tongue but that You, O LORD, already know all of it.
4.amp: For there is not a word [millah] in my tongue [lashon], but, lo, O LORD [YHWH], You know [yada] it altogether [kol].
4.notes: The audit reaches speech before speech exists: the millah (H4405) still on the lashon (H3956), unspoken, is already fully known — kol, all of it, root and motive included. Every careless word is pre-read (cf. Matthew 12:36).

5.text: You have hemmed me in, behind and before, and You have laid Your hand upon me.
5.amp: You have beset [tsur — besieged, enclosed] me behind [achor] and before [qedem], and laid [shith] Your hand [kaph] upon me.
5.notes: tsur (H6696) is siege-language: enclosed rear and front, past and future both held. Yet the verse ends not with walls but with a kaph (H3709), an open palm laid on — the same word for a blessing hand; whether the hemming feels like siege or shelter depends on whose hand it is.

6.text: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me — too high; I cannot climb to it.
6.amp: Such knowledge [daat] is too wonderful [pilah — beyond comprehension] for me; it is high [sagab — set inaccessibly high], I cannot [yakol] attain unto it.
6.notes: The creature's honest response to being fully known: not resentment but vertigo. pilah (H6383) is wonder past understanding, sagab (H7682) the unscalable height — the doctrine is confessed precisely by admitting it cannot be climbed (cf. Romans 11:33).

7.text: Where could I go from Your Spirit? Where could I flee from Your face?
7.amp: Whither shall I go [yalak] from Your Spirit [ruach]? or whither shall I flee [barach] from Your presence [panim]?
7.notes: The second stanza opens with the fugitive's two questions — yalak and barach (H1272), go and flee — and the psalm now runs every escape route to its end. Jonah tried this experimentally and confirmed the findings (cf. Jonah 1:3).

8.text: If I climb up to heaven, You are there; if I spread my bed in Sheol — look, You are there.
8.amp: If I ascend up [nasaq] into heaven [shamayim], You are there: if I make my bed [yatsa] in hell [sheol — the realm of the dead], behold, You are there.
8.notes: The vertical axis tested at both extremes: shamayim and sheol (H8064, H7585) — and the answer is identical, attah sham, You are there. Even the grave is not away from God; for the believer that is the gospel before the gospel (cf. Psalm 23:4).

9.text: If I take the wings of the dawn and settle at the farthest edge of the sea,
9.amp: If I take [nasa] the wings [kanaph] of the morning [shachar — the dawn], and dwell [shakan] in the uttermost parts [acharit] of the sea [yam];
9.notes: The horizontal axis: riding the kanaph shachar (H3671, H7837) — dawn's light racing west at the speed only light travels — to the acharit yam (H319, H3220), the Mediterranean's far rim, the west end of an Israelite's world. The most beautiful escape plan ever written, and it fails.

10.text: even there Your hand would lead me, and Your right hand would keep its hold on me.
10.amp: Even there shall Your hand [yad] lead [nachah] me, and Your right hand [yamin] shall hold [achaz — grasp fast] me.
10.notes: The fugitive arrives at the world's edge to find not a wall but a hand: nachah (H5148), the shepherd's leading-verb, and achaz (H270), the grip that does not slip. The pursuit was guidance all along — what he fled was holding him up.

11.text: If I say, 'Surely the darkness will crush down and cover me, and the light around me become night,'
11.amp: If I say [amar], 'Surely the darkness [choshek] shall cover [shuph — overwhelm, bruise] me; even the night [layil] shall be light [or] about me [baad];'
11.notes: The last resort: not distance but concealment — let choshek (H2822) swallow me. The covering-verb (H7779) is the bruising-word of Genesis 3:15: darkness invoked as a crushing blanket. The plan is hopeless for the reason verse 12 gives.

12.text: even the darkness is not dark to You: the night shines like the day, for darkness and light are both alike to You.
12.amp: Yea, the darkness [choshek] hides ['darkeneth', chashak, the KJV margin] not from You; but the night [layil] shines [or] as the day [yom]: the darkness and the light [orah] are both alike to You ['as is the darkness, so is the light', the KJV margin].
12.notes: God has no night vision because He needs none: to Him layil IS or (H3915, H216), night is light. The sun of Psalm 19 rules our seeing; the Maker's sight is unconditioned. Every hidden thing lives in broad day (cf. Hebrews 4:13; Daniel 2:22).

13.text: For You Yourself acquired my inmost parts; You wove me together in my mother's womb.
13.amp: For You have possessed [qanah — acquired, created] my reins [kilyah — my kidneys, my inmost being]: You have covered [sakak — woven, screened] me in my mother's [em] womb [beten].
13.notes: The third stanza gives the reason for the total knowledge: authorship. qanah (H7069) is to acquire and create — the kilyah (H3629), the kidneys, Hebrew's seat of the deepest self, His from the start. sakak (H5526), the hedging-verb of Job 1:10, here as weaving: knit together in the beten (H990), person before daylight.

14.text: I praise You, because I am fearfully and wonderfully made — set apart in the making. Marvelous are Your works, and my soul knows it full well.
14.amp: I will praise [yadah] You; for I am fearfully [yare] and wonderfully made [palah — distinguished, made distinct]: marvellous [pala — wonderful beyond ability] are Your works [maaseh]; and that my soul [nephesh] knows [yada] right well ['greatly', meod, the KJV margin].
14.notes: yare and palah (H3372, H6395): made in a way that inspires awe, and made DISTINCT — no interchangeable parts, no duplicate persons. pala (H6381) is the miracle-word of the Exodus applied to ordinary human anatomy. The nephesh knows it meod, exceedingly — self-knowledge as doxology.

15.text: My frame was not hidden from You when I was being made in the secret place, embroidered in the depths of the earth.
15.amp: My substance ['strength, body', otsem, the KJV margin — my frame, my bones] was not hid [kachad] from You, when I was made [asah] in secret [sether], and curiously wrought [raqam — embroidered, woven in colors] in the lowest parts [tachti] of the earth [eretz].
15.notes: raqam (H7551) is the embroiderer's verb, used of the tabernacle's woven work (cf. Exodus 26:36): veins, nerves, and sinews as colored needlework. The sether (H5643), the womb's hidden place, pictured as earth's depths — hidden from every eye but One; nothing about the unborn was ever hidden from God.

16.text: Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in Your book all my days were written — the days shaped for me when not one of them yet existed.
16.amp: Your eyes [ayin] did see [raah] my substance, yet being unperfect [golem — the unformed mass, the embryo]; and in Your book [sepher] all my members were written [kathab], which in continuance were fashioned [yatsar — 'what days they should be fashioned', the KJV margin], when as yet there was none [echad] of them.
16.notes: golem (H1564): the embryo, the not-yet-formed — seen, known, and already on record. The sepher (H5612) holds the days themselves, yatsar (H3335), formed like pottery before one existed: biography written before birth. The strongest single verse in Scripture on the personhood of the unborn and the ordination of our days (cf. Job 14:5; Ephesians 2:10).

17.text: How precious are Your thoughts toward me, O God! How vast the sum of them is!
17.amp: How precious [yaqar — prized, weighty] also are Your thoughts [rea] unto me, O God [El]! how great [atsam — mighty, numerous] is the sum [rosh] of them!
17.notes: The surveillance that a guilty conscience would dread, the psalmist prizes: yaqar (H3365), precious. His thoughts toward me — the same rea (H7454) He read from afar in verse 2 — are now the treasure; being fully known by perfect love converts from threat to wealth.

18.text: If I tried to count them, they would outnumber the sand. I awake — and I am still with You.
18.amp: If I should count [saphar] them, they are more in number [rabah] than the sand [chol]: when I awake [quts], I am still [od] with You.
18.notes: saphar (H5608), the counting-verb, defeated by chol (H2344), the sand — Abraham's own uncountable measure. And the loveliest waking line in Scripture: the count abandoned in sleep resumes at dawn exactly where everything always is — od immakh, still with You.

19.text: Oh that You would slay the wicked, O God! Depart from me, you men of blood,
19.amp: Surely You will slay [qatal] the wicked [rasha], O God [Eloah]: depart [sur] from me therefore, you bloody [dam] men [enosh] —
19.notes: The jarring stanza — and honest: a man who treasures God's total knowledge cannot shrug at those who trample it. The plea is for GOD to act (qatal, H6991 is His verb, not David's), and David's own move is separation: sur (H5493), depart — distance from the men of dam (H1818), of bloods.

20.text: who speak against You with malicious intent; Your enemies lift up Your name for a lie.
20.amp: For they speak [amar] against You wickedly [mezimmah — with scheming intent], and Your enemies [ar] take [nasa] Your name in vain [shav — for emptiness, for the lie].
20.notes: The charge is verbal treason: mezimmah (H4209), premeditated scheming, and the Name nasa la-shav (H7723) — lifted for emptiness, the third commandment's own wording (cf. Exodus 20:7). David's quarrel with them is God's honor, not his own grievances.

21.text: Do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD? Do I not loathe those who rise up against You?
21.amp: Do not I hate [sane] them, O LORD [YHWH], that hate [sane] You? and am not I grieved [qut — filled with loathing] with those that rise up [tequmah] against You?
21.notes: Covenant alignment stated in the old covenant's strongest idiom: sane (H8130) — their war on God makes neutrality impossible, and qut (H6962) is grief that turns the stomach. The Christian reads this zeal through the cross, where the Enemy-lover died for enemies (cf. Matthew 5:44; Romans 5:10) — hating the rebellion while praying for the rebels.

22.text: With complete hatred I hate them; I count them my own enemies.
22.amp: I hate [sane] them with perfect [taklith — complete, utter] hatred [sinah]: I count them mine enemies [oyeb].
22.notes: taklith (H8503): hatred at full completeness — total identification with God's cause, no private malice named anywhere in it. And the very next verse shows where such zeal must immediately look: inward.

23.text: Search me through, O God, and know my heart; put me to the test, and know my anxious thoughts,
23.amp: Search [chaqar] me, O God [El], and know [yada] my heart [lebab]: try [bachan — test as metal is assayed] me, and know my thoughts [sarappim — my anxious, branching thoughts]:
23.notes: The psalm's masterstroke: the chaqar of verse 1, which no one can escape, is now INVITED. bachan (H974) is the assayer's fire, and the sarappim (H8312) are the disquieting, branching thoughts — the anxieties. The man who condemned God's enemies submits his own lebab to the same court first.

24.text: and see if there is any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.
24.amp: And see [raah] if there be any wicked ['way of pain, or, grief', otseb, the KJV margin] way [derek] in me, and lead [nachah] me in the way [derek] everlasting [olam].
24.notes: The derek otseb (H6090), the way of pain — any road in me that ends in grief or gives it. And the final petition hands the whole psalm its destination: nachah (H5148), the shepherd-verb of verse 10, on the derek olam (H5769) — the ancient road that outlasts every other way, walked with the Guide who has known me from the womb to the world's far edge.
